weaknesses: The central claim of producing functional, reproducible implementations is not adequately validated. Most results are subjective LLM-judge scores; experiments are not run to reproduce reported metrics. The executability study uses only five manually selected repositories, leaves successful execution undefined, and measures edited lines rather than scientific correctness.

Paper2Code is strongly selection-biased: it includes only papers with public repositories below 70,000 tokens and then retains the 30 highest-scoring repositories per venue according to an LLM judge. This poorly represents the motivating code-unavailable setting and may favor unusually easy or well-documented papers. Possible training contamination from public 2024 papers and repositories is not investigated.

The evaluation protocol is internally inconsistent. Section 4.3 identifies o3-mini-high as the evaluator, whereas Appendix A.3 and the benchmark tables identify GPT-4o. Using o3-mini-high both to generate and judge its outputs would also create self-preference concerns. Exact judge prompts are missing.

Baseline fairness is unclear. PaperCoder uses many high-reasoning model calls and generates substantially more code, but token budgets, costs, context handling, retries, temperatures, and matched compute are not reported. PaperCoder has no uncertainty estimate on PaperBench, while competing results are averaged over three runs.

Technical novelty is limited to a tailored sequence of prompting stages resembling established software-engineering workflows. There is no execution feedback, automated testing, debugging, search, or substantive inter-agent collaboration. The experiments do not isolate structural benefits from simply using more calls, context, and output tokens.

The cumulative ablation does not support the claim that every component contributes: architecture design lowers both scores, and configuration generation lowers the reference-free score. It also confounds component effects with increasing compute and context.

The human study is too small and weakly controlled for the claims made: each paper appears to have one evaluator, participants inspect ten repositories in roughly 45 minutes without executing them, and repeated repositories across groups can undermine anonymization. Inter-rater reliability and statistical tests are absent; compensation remains the placeholder "$X," and consent or ethics-review details are not given.

Reproducibility and reporting quality are insufficient. No implementation, generated repositories, raw judgments, or complete evaluation configuration is linked. Architecture design decreases both scores and configuration generation decreases the reference-free score, contradicting the claim that every component contributes; leave-one-component-out and budget-controlled ablations are needed.

The methodological novelty is modest relative to established planning-and-coding agent workflows. Given the evaluation, contamination, and executability issues, the current evidence does not make this otherwise promising system competitive for acceptance at a top-tier venue.
